Customer Churn Intelligence System

Predict who leaves. Explain why. Put a value on keeping them.
Abhishek Rai A.
USN 24SEAI003  ·  V Semester, AI&ML  ·  Mysore University School of Engineering, University of Mysore
Mentor: Dr. Santhosh Kumar K. S.
Good morning everyone. I am Abhishek Rai A., fifth semester AI and ML. My talk is about the capstone of my summer internship at Bluemind Solutions: a customer churn intelligence system. Dr. Santhosh Kumar K. S. mentored the work. The picture on the right is the problem in one image. Every dot is a customer. Blue ones stay, orange ones leave. 53 of these 200 dots leave, which is 26.5 percent, the real churn rate in my data.
1 in 4
customers walked away.
0 of 7,043 customers left. That is 26.5%, and every one of them is monthly revenue that stops.
Churn means a customer cancels the service. In this dataset 1,869 of 7,043 customers left. That is 26.5 percent, about one in four. Every one of them is monthly revenue that stops. If asked whether this is real company data: it is IBM's public Telco Customer Churn sample dataset, not Bluemind's data.
A retention team can only call so many people.
Who is about to leave,
and why?
A retention team can only call so many people. So the useful question is not how many customers will leave. It is who is about to leave, and why. That question is what this project answers.

I will give you the result first, so you know where this is going. The model ranks customers it has never seen with a ROC-AUC of 0.847. At my chosen cutoff it catches 82 percent of the customers who leave, 306 of 374. And the estimate of what that could keep is up to 179 thousand dollars a year. That last number rests on an assumption, and I will be open about it when we get there. The plan: the problem, related work, the data, the models, the impact, and the dashboard. About twenty minutes.

The project
Predict.

Explain.

Value.

The project covers the full applied cycle in four parts. Predict with a LightGBM model. Explain each prediction with SHAP. Put a dollar value on the result. And deploy it as a dashboard that someone other than me can use. Many projects stop at the first step. I wanted to reach the last one.
Related work

Nine studies shaped this project.

Chosen from 36 references. What each one found, and what I took from it.
I read 36 references, and nine shaped this project most. They are on a timeline from 2006 to 2022. Hung, Yen and Wang, 2006: decision trees and neural networks both predicted churn well, so tree models are in my comparison. Burez and Van den Poel, 2009: class imbalance needs care, so I used class weights, stratified splits and ROC-AUC. Verbeke and colleagues, 2012: judge churn models by profit, so I added a dollar estimate. Kaufman and colleagues, 2012: how data leakage happens, so I split the data before fitting anything. Vafeiadis and colleagues, 2015: SVM with AdaBoost was best, accuracy almost 97 percent, so I compared model families against a baseline and reported more than accuracy. Saito and Rehmsmeier, 2015: the precision-recall plot says more than ROC when positives are rare, so my cutoff comes from the precision-recall curve. Lundberg and Lee, 2017: SHAP explains any model, so I explain every customer. Ahmad and colleagues, 2019: XGBoost was best on SyriaTel data with AUC 93.3 percent, so XGBoost is one of my four tuned models. Grinsztajn and colleagues, 2022: tree models stayed ahead of deep learning on tables of about 10,000 rows, so I used boosted trees, not a neural network, for 7,043 rows.
The data
0
customers. 19 features each.
IBM's public Telco Customer Churn sample. One row per customer, plus one label: did they leave?
Who they are
Gender, senior citizen, partner, dependents
Their account
Tenure, contract, paperless billing, payment method
The services they use
Phone, multiple lines, internet, online security, online backup, device protection, tech support, streaming TV, streaming movies
Their bill
Monthly charges, total charges
This is IBM's public Telco Customer Churn dataset. Each row is one customer, with 19 usable features: who they are, their account, the services they use, and their bill. Plus one label: did they leave or not. If asked why 19 when the file has 21 columns: one is the customer ID, which I dropped, and one is the Churn label. If asked about cleaning: TotalCharges arrives as text and is blank for 11 brand new customers with tenure 0. I filled it with monthly charges times tenure, which uses only that row, so nothing leaks.
The data

Split first. Test once.

80% to learn from. 20% locked away until the very end, with the same churn share on both sides.
0
customers to train and tune
0
held out for the test
Locked until the end
Each dot stands for about 70 customers. Orange dots are customers who left.
Before fitting anything, I split the data 80 and 20, with the same share of churners on both sides. That is called a stratified split. 5,634 customers are for training and tuning. 1,409 are locked away and used only once, for the final test. So the scaler, the encoder and the models never see the test customers. If asked about the charts on the next slides: they use all 7,043 rows to describe the data, but no model was fitted on test rows.

the riskiest group
This is the strongest single pattern in the data. 42.7 percent of month-to-month customers left, against 11.3 percent on one-year contracts and 2.8 percent on two-year contracts. That is about fifteen times as many. A short commitment makes it easy to walk away. If asked whether the contract causes churn: I cannot claim that. Customers who are unsure probably choose a monthly contract in the first place. It is a strong signal, not a proven cause.

Two more patterns. Churn is highest in the first six months, at 52.9 percent, and falls steadily to 9.5 percent for customers who have stayed four years or more. And customers who left were paying more: 74.4 dollars a month on average, against 61.3 dollars for those who stayed. So the risky profile is visible even before any model: new, on a monthly contract, with a high bill.

Six steps. The split comes first, so the scaler and the encoder never see the test rows. Cleaning and encoding sit inside one scikit-learn Pipeline: StandardScaler for the numbers and OneHotEncoder for the categories. Then I tune four models, choose a cutoff, explain with SHAP, and deploy. The dashboard loads the same saved pipeline, so what I tested is exactly what gets used. If asked why I scale when tree models do not need it: logistic regression does need it, and one shared preprocessing step keeps the comparison fair.
Modelling

LightGBM wins. Narrowly.

Cross-validated ROC-AUC, 5 folds. The bars start at 0.5, which is random guessing.

To be upfront: the untuned baseline scored 0.842 on the test set, so it is not in this cross-validation chart.
All four within 0.003.
So the cutoff and the explanation matter more than the model.
I tuned four models with randomized search and 5-fold cross-validation, scored on ROC-AUC. All four land within 0.003 of each other. LightGBM scored highest, 0.8488, so I selected it. But I will not pretend it is far ahead. The choice of model mattered less here than the cutoff and the explanation. The bars start at 0.5 because that is what random guessing scores. To be upfront: my untuned logistic regression baseline scored 0.842, but that was on the test set, so it does not belong in a cross-validation chart. If asked why ROC-AUC: the classes are imbalanced, and ROC-AUC does not depend on any single cutoff. If asked why LightGBM when it is nearly a tie: top score, fast to train, and it works directly with SHAP's tree explainer.
Modelling

It ranks unseen customers well.

0.000
ROC-AUC on 1,409 customers it never saw.
Pick one customer who left and one who stayed. The model ranks the leaver higher 85 times out of 100.
Cross-validation 0.849. Test 0.847. They agree.
On the 1,409 customers the model never saw, the ROC-AUC is 0.847. In plain words: if I take one customer who left and one who stayed, the model gives the leaver the higher score about 85 times out of 100. Cross-validation gave 0.849, so the test result agrees with it. The untuned baseline scored 0.842 on the same test set, so tuning added about 0.005. That is a small gain, and I say so plainly. The orange dot on the curve is the cutoff I chose, which comes next. If asked what the axes are: across is the share of stayers flagged by mistake, up is the share of leavers caught, at every possible cutoff.
Modelling

Cutoff 0.485. Chosen, not assumed.

To be upfront: I picked this cutoff on the test set, so these three scores can be a little optimistic.
Cutoff
0.200

0.00
F1
A missed leaver costs more than a wasted offer, so I accept more false alarms to catch more leavers.
The model gives every customer a score between 0 and 1, and the cutoff decides who gets flagged. The usual default is 0.5, but I did not want to assume it. Watch the line sweep: as the cutoff moves, precision and recall trade against each other. Missing a real leaver costs more than a wasted offer, so I took the cutoff where F1 is highest. That is 0.485. There the model catches 82 percent of leavers, and the price is a precision of 53 percent. To be upfront: I picked this cutoff using the test set, so these scores can be a little optimistic. The clean way is to pick it on validation data and then test once. If asked why F1: it balances precision and recall in one number. A real business would set the cutoff from the cost of an offer and the value of a saved customer, which I did not have.

Every dot here is one of the 1,409 test customers, coloured by what really happened: orange left, blue stayed. They sort themselves by what the model said at my cutoff. Of the 374 who really left, the model caught 306 and missed 68. Of the 1,035 who stayed, it left 762 alone and flagged 273 by mistake. Those false alarms are the price of catching more leavers. In total 579 customers are flagged. Accuracy is 76 percent, but a model that says nobody leaves would already score 73.5 percent, so accuracy alone says very little here. That is why I report recall and precision.

Explaining the model

What drives a customer to leave.

Pushes risk up

01Month-to-month contract
02Short tenure
03No online security
04High monthly charges
05No tech support
06Fiber optic internet
07Pays by electronic check

Pushes risk down

One-year and two-year contracts
SHAP shows how each feature pushes a prediction up or down. On the left, every dot is one test customer, and dots to the right of the centre line push the risk up. A month-to-month contract is the strongest driver, then short tenure, no online security, a high monthly bill, no tech support, fiber optic internet and payment by electronic check. One-year and two-year contracts push the risk down. This agrees with what the raw data showed earlier, which is reassuring. If asked what SHAP is: it splits each prediction into a contribution from every feature, based on Shapley values from game theory. The contributions plus a base value add up to the model's output. If asked whether these are causes: no. SHAP explains the model, not the world.
Explaining one customer

Why this customer scores 95.3%.

Highest risk
in the whole test set
Month-to-month contract

This is the highest-risk customer in the test set, with a predicted churn probability of 95.3 percent. The bars build up the score one feature at a time. The month-to-month contract adds the most, then a tenure of only one month, then the high bill of 95 dollars, no online security and no tech support. A retention team can read this and know what to offer. A bare score does not allow that. If asked about the bar values: they are in log-odds, not percent. They start from a base of minus 0.641 and add up to 3.011, which converts to 95.3 percent. If asked whether 95.3 percent is a true probability: it is the model's score. I trained with balanced class weights, which pushes scores upward, so I would calibrate before quoting it as a real-world probability.

To be upfront: the 35% is my assumption, the cost of the offers is not subtracted, and the 579 include 273 false alarms. So this is an upper estimate.
the best case, not a promise
Now the money. The model flags 579 customers, and they pay 73.79 dollars a month on average. That is 42,724 dollars of monthly bills at risk. If a retention offer works on 35 percent of them, about 14,954 dollars a month is kept, which is 179,442 dollars a year, roughly 179 thousand. I want to be upfront about three things. The 35 percent is my assumption, not a measured figure. I have not subtracted the cost of the offers. And the 579 flagged customers include 273 false alarms who were not leaving. So please treat 179 thousand as an upper estimate, not a promise. If asked why dollars: the dataset is American and in US dollars.

The model sits behind a Streamlit dashboard. You fill in a customer's details and press one button. You get a churn probability, a bar that shows where the cutoff sits, and a plain high or low risk flag. This example customer scores 50.4 percent, just above the cutoff, so the dashboard recommends a retention offer. It loads the same saved pipeline I tested in the notebook. If asked why the screen says threshold 0.48: the stored cutoff is 0.4848. The dashboard shows two decimals. If asked about the form: it asks for 14 of the 19 fields. The other five service fields are set to No. The batch tab takes all 19. If asked whether it is online: it runs from Colab through a temporary link. A permanent link is a next step.
Deployment

Bad rows are stopped, not scored.

Clean file, 8 rows
8scored
3flagged high risk
File with planted errors, 12 rows
0scored
0flagged high risk
0rejected, with a reason
The batch tab scores a whole CSV file, but it checks every row first. I tested it with a file of 12 rows where I planted errors on purpose: a negative tenure, a tenure of 250 months, a senior citizen value of 2, a zero bill, a 999 dollar bill, a negative total, the word twelve instead of a number, and an empty row. All 8 bad rows are rejected with a reason and never scored. The other 4 are scored, and 3 of them are flagged high risk. In the clean test file all 8 customers were scored and 3 were flagged. If asked what gets fixed instead of rejected: extra spaces or different capital letters in category values are corrected, like the lowercase row here. A blank total charge is filled the same way as in training. If asked about the Crypto Wallet row: an unknown category is ignored for that field and the row is still scored. A stricter version would warn about it.
Context

Beside published work.

For this project, F1, recall and precision are for the churn class. A missing bar means the study did not report that measure.
Vafeiadis et al. (2015), UCI data
Ahmad et al. (2019), SyriaTel data
This project, IBM Telco data
Accuracy if nobody is predicted to leave (73.5%)
Accuracy is the weakest basis.
Saying "nobody leaves" already scores 73.5% on my data.
Ahmad et al. had richer data.
An operator's own records, with usage and call history.
NOT A RANKING
Here are the headline scores the two closest studies reported, next to mine. Vafeiadis and colleagues report accuracy of almost 97 percent and an F-measure above 84 percent. Ahmad and colleagues report an AUC of 93.3 percent. My test ROC-AUC is 84.7 percent, recall 81.8 percent, precision 52.8 percent, F1 64.2 percent and accuracy 75.8 percent. This is not a ranking. The datasets and measures differ. Accuracy is the weakest basis for comparison: on my data, saying that nobody leaves is already 73.5 percent accurate, the dashed line, and my 75.8 percent comes from a cutoff chosen to favour recall. The higher AUC of Ahmad and colleagues comes from an operator's own, much richer records, and my error analysis agrees: my worst mistakes are customers whose reasons for leaving are not in the table.
Context

This project joins the parts.

An empty cell means the point is not reported in the summary of Table 1.1, not that the study ignored it. The ring is a part cover: the dollar value assumes a 35% success rate.
This chart compares what each study covers, as summarised in Table 1.1 of my report. The earlier studies each handle one or two parts of the problem well: Burez and Van den Poel class imbalance, Verbeke and colleagues profit, and Vafeiadis and colleagues and Ahmad and colleagues boosted models. This project brings these parts together in one pipeline and adds explanations for single customers and a working dashboard. Its weak point is the money estimate, which assumes a 35 percent success rate and leaves out the cost of the offers. That is why it is only a ring, a part cover. The cutoff is not yet chosen by cost, as Verbraken and colleagues suggest. Boosted trees came out on top, as in Ahmad and colleagues and Grinsztajn and colleagues, but LightGBM led logistic regression by only 0.0026 in cross-validated ROC-AUC, 0.8488 against 0.8462, which should not be read as a real win. If asked about empty cells: an empty cell means the point is not in my summary of that study, not that the study ignored it.
Honest limits

Four limits. Four next steps.

Limit
What I would do next
The cutoff was chosen on the test set
Choose it on validation folds, then test once
Random split, not tested on a later period
Walk-forward validation, and a survival model for when a customer leaves
The dollar figure rests on an assumed 35%
A permanent dashboard link, so a real team can measure the real rate
No usage or support-call data
A weekly scoring job that sends the high-risk list to the CRM
Four limits, stated plainly, and what I would do about each. One: the cutoff was chosen on the test set, so next time I would choose it on validation folds. Two: the split is random, not time-based, so the next step is walk-forward validation, and a survival model that predicts when a customer will leave. Three: the dollar figure rests on an assumed 35 percent, so a permanent dashboard link would let a real team measure the real rate. Four: there is no usage or support-call data, so a weekly scoring job feeding the CRM is the way to bring this into real use.

To close. In twenty working days I went from NumPy basics to an explainable machine learning system with its own dashboard. The model reaches a test ROC-AUC of 0.847 and catches 82 percent of the customers who leave. The estimate is up to 179 thousand dollars a year, with the assumptions I named. Backup slide. Precision asks how many of my flags were right. Recall asks how many of the real leavers I found. F1 balances the two. Accuracy counts every correct call, which is why it looks fine even for a useless model when most customers stay. ROC-AUC does not use a cutoff at all.
